Clinical Reference

Hypomagnesemia

On this page
Serum magnesium below 1.7 mg/dL (< 0.7 mmol/L) — almost always true total-body depletion from GI or renal loss, occasionally redistribution. Most cases are mild and silent, but severe depletion (< 1.0–1.2 mg/dL) causes tetany, seizures, and torsades de pointes, and low Mg is the reason a potassium or calcium won't correct. The reflex is replete magnesium → and the K⁺ and Ca²⁺ follow → then find and fix the cause.
Low Mg < 1.7 mg/dL (< 0.7 mmol/L) Severe < 1.0–1.2 mg/dL Tetany · long QT → torsades Give Mg → unlocks K⁺ & Ca²⁺ ~1% of body Mg is in serum ICU prevalence ~50–65%
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Magnesium is the body's fourth-most-abundant cation and the second-most-abundant intracellular one. Total-body magnesium is about 24 g (~1000 mmol), distributed roughly 60% in bone, ~38% in muscle and soft tissue (intracellular), and only ~1% in the extracellular fluid — of which about 0.3% is in the serum you measure. That single fact drives everything downstream: because the serum holds such a trivial fraction, a normal serum magnesium does not exclude a large total-body deficit, and a falling serum value can mean the tank is nearly empty. Roughly 30% of serum magnesium is bound to albumin and ~60–70% is free (ionized) and physiologically active — but unlike calcium, correcting Mg for albumin is not standard practice.

Magnesium is a silent cofactor for > 300 enzymes — every reaction that uses ATP actually uses Mg-ATP, so magnesium quietly powers the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, kinases, and the machinery of DNA/protein synthesis. It also sits in the pore of the NMDA receptor and gates several ion channels. When magnesium runs low, two things happen at once: energy-dependent pumps falter, and membranes become hyperexcitable — the substrate for tetany, seizures, and arrhythmia.

How the body handles magnesium (three organs). The gut absorbs ~30–40% of a ~360 mg daily intake, mostly passively across the small bowel but fine-tuned by the TRPM6/TRPM7 channels in the ileum and colon — the same channels that proton-pump inhibitors down-regulate. The bone is a slow reservoir that does not release magnesium quickly, so it cannot buffer an acute drop. The kidney is the master regulator: ~95% of filtered magnesium is reabsorbed, the bulk (~70%) paracellularly in the thick ascending limb (driven by the lumen-positive voltage that the NKCC2 transporter creates — the same voltage a loop diuretic abolishes), with final fine-tuning (~10%) transcellularly through TRPM6 in the distal convoluted tubule. A healthy kidney can cut urinary magnesium to almost nothing, so dietary deficiency alone rarely causes hypomagnesemia unless there are ongoing GI or renal losses.

Why magnesium is the hidden lever for potassium. Intracellular magnesium normally blocks the renal outer-medullary potassium channel (ROMK) from the cytoplasmic side, restraining potassium secretion in the distal nephron. When magnesium is depleted, that block is released and the tubule leaks potassium relentlessly — which is why hypokalemia with hypomagnesemia is refractory to potassium alone. You can pour KCl in and it pours straight out in the urine until magnesium is replaced. This is the single highest-yield teaching point in the whole topic: check and replace magnesium in any refractory hypokalemia.

Why magnesium is also the hidden lever for calcium. Magnesium is required for PTH secretion and for end-organ responsiveness to PTH. Paradoxically, severe hypomagnesemia (< ~1.0 mg/dL) impairs PTH release and creates PTH resistance, producing a hypocalcemia that will not correct with calcium or vitamin D until the magnesium is repleted. (Mild hypomagnesemia can transiently stimulate PTH — it is the severe range that shuts it down.) So the classic "refractory hypocalcemia" of the alcoholic or the malnourished patient is a magnesium problem wearing a calcium mask.

Why the heart and neuromuscular junction are the organs at risk. Low magnesium destabilizes membranes and prolongs cardiac repolarization — on the ECG this is a prolonged QT (often with the accompanying hypokalemia/hypocalcemia), widened QRS, prolonged PR, and flattened T waves, with early afterdepolarizations that trigger torsades de pointes and ventricular fibrillation. Magnesium also potentiates digoxin toxicity (both impair the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase). At the neuromuscular junction, low magnesium increases acetylcholine release and lowers the threshold for depolarization, producing tremor, hyperreflexia, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, carpopedal spasm, and seizures — the same tetany you see in hypocalcemia, here compounded by the magnesium-dependent hypocalcemia itself.

Think of magnesium as the master key on the electrolyte keychain. Potassium and calcium each have their own lock (their own channels and hormones), but magnesium is the key that has to turn first: it unlocks the ROMK "drain valve" so the kidney will hold onto potassium, and it unlocks the PTH "thermostat" so calcium can be defended. If the master key is missing, you can jiggle the potassium and calcium locks all day — pour in KCl, push calcium gluconate — and nothing catches, because the mechanism they depend on is jammed. Replace the magnesium, and suddenly both other locks turn on their own. And because the serum is just the doorknob and the real magnesium lives deep inside the house (bone and muscle), the knob can feel almost normal while the rooms are empty.
Only ~1% of body magnesium is extracellular and only ~0.3% is in serum — so serum Mg is a late, insensitive marker of a deficit that lives in bone and muscle. The urinary fractional excretion (FEMg) splits the two loss routes.
The three failure modes of low magnesium. Because both the potassium and calcium defects are mechanistically downstream of magnesium, replacing K⁺ or Ca²⁺ alone fails — repleting magnesium is what lets them correct.
The nephron. ~70% of filtered magnesium is reabsorbed paracellularly in the thick ascending limb (loop diuretics abolish the driving voltage → Mg wasting); the DCT does the final ~10% through TRPM6 (the channel PPIs and cisplatin injure).
BruceBlaus, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — File:Nephron Anatomy.png
Elemental magnesium — the fourth-most-abundant cation in the body and a cofactor for > 300 ATP-dependent enzymes, including the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase that every excitable cell depends on.
Warut Roonguthai, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — File:Magnesium crystals.jpg
Every therapy in this guide maps to one step in the story above. IV/oral magnesium salts refill the depleted cofactor. Amiloride closes the ENaC channel in the collecting duct, lowering the lumen-negative voltage that drives ongoing renal magnesium (and potassium) wasting — the tool for chronic renal wasters. Stopping the offender (deprescribing a PPI, lowering a loop diuretic, holding cisplatin) removes the drain. And giving magnesium before or with potassium and calcium is not a courtesy — it is the mechanistic prerequisite that lets those repletions actually hold.
📊

Definitions, units, and severity bands

There is no validated numeric severity score for hypomagnesemia (unlike CHA₂DS₂-VASc for AF). Severity is graded by the level, symptoms, and the company it keeps (hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, arrhythmia). Watch the units — magnesium is reported three different ways and the numbers look nothing alike.

BandSerum Mg (mg/dL)mmol/LmEq/LTypical clinical meaning
Normal1.7–2.20.70–0.951.4–1.8Reference range (labs vary 1.7–2.4)
Mild1.2–1.70.5–0.71.0–1.4Usually asymptomatic; oral repletion, find cause
Moderate1.0–1.20.4–0.50.8–1.0Symptoms emerge; usually IV repletion
Severe< 1.0< 0.4< 0.8Tetany, seizures, arrhythmia — IV, monitored
Unit conversions (memorize these)1 mmol/L = 2 mEq/L = 2.43 mg/dL. To convert mg/dL → mmol/L multiply by 0.411; mg/dL → mEq/L multiply by 0.823. So a serum Mg of "0.5 mmol/L" is a scary 1.2 mg/dL, and "1.0 mEq/L" is 1.2 mg/dL — always confirm which unit your lab uses before you panic or reassure. The unit converter in the Clinic workup does the arithmetic for you.

Molecular note: magnesium is divalent, so its mEq value is twice its mmol value; the mg/dL value uses its atomic weight (24.3). Ionized (free) magnesium can be measured directly but is not widely available; total serum Mg is the standard test and is not routinely corrected for albumin.

🩺 Clinic — outpatient recognition & chronic repletion
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Who is at risk & how it presents

Outpatient hypomagnesemia is usually the fingerprint of a drug, a gut, or a drink: a proton-pump inhibitor, a loop or thiazide diuretic, chronic diarrhea/malabsorption, or alcohol use disorder. It is common but under-checked — magnesium is not on the basic metabolic panel, so it is missed unless you deliberately order it. The highest-yield populations to test: patients with refractory hypokalemia or hypocalcemia (the loudest clue), type 2 diabetics (renal wasting; worsened by SGLT2/loop use), patients on long-term PPIs with cramps or arrhythmia, alcohol use disorder, and anyone on cisplatin, cetuximab, aminoglycosides, amphotericin, or calcineurin inhibitors (transplant patients).

Reality checkMost mild hypomagnesemia is asymptomatic and found incidentally — often only because someone finally sent the level while chasing a potassium or calcium that would not correct. The two things that convert it from a lab curiosity into a threat are an ECG-relevant comorbidity (digoxin, heart failure, prior MI, QT-prolonging drugs) and concurrent electrolyte depletion (hypokalemia/hypocalcemia), which is present in roughly 40–60% of significant cases.

Presentation — symptom / sign, approximate frequency, and why

Symptom / sign~ FrequencyWhy it happens (mechanism)

Tremor, hyperreflexia, Chvostek / Trousseau signs15–40%*Increased neuromuscular excitability (compounded by the Mg-dependent hypocalcemia) → latent/overt tetany

Percentages are approximate relative prominences among symptomatic patients, not validated epidemiology. Treat the level, the trajectory, and the companions — not just the complaint.

Chvostek sign — tapping over the facial nerve (CN VII, shown) just anterior to the ear triggers an ipsilateral facial twitch, a marker of the neuromuscular hyperexcitability of low Mg/Ca. Trousseau sign (carpopedal spasm with BP-cuff inflation) is more specific.

Long-term proton-pump inhibitors down-regulate intestinal TRPM6/7 and are a leading, reversible outpatient cause — the FDA issued a formal safety warning in 2011. Check a Mg in any chronic-PPI patient with cramps, palpitations, or a low K⁺/Ca²⁺.

Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs — and what each result changes

Serum magnesiumThe test is only useful if you order it — Mg is not on the BMP/CMP. Send it in anyone with refractory hypokalemia/hypocalcemia, on a PPI/diuretic/cisplatin, alcohol use disorder, or unexplained arrhythmia. Remember serum Mg underestimates total-body depletion.First
Potassium, calcium (ionized), phosphateThe "traveling companions." A refractory low K⁺ or Ca²⁺ is often the reason to check Mg in the first place — and you cannot fix them until Mg is corrected.Initial
Intact PTH (if hypocalcemic)Severe hypomagnesemia gives an inappropriately low/normal PTH despite hypocalcemia (functional hypoparathyroidism) — a diagnostic fingerprint that reverses with Mg repletion.If low Ca
12-lead ECGOrder now if Mg is low with symptoms, on digoxin, or with heart disease. Look for prolonged PR, widened QRS, prolonged QT, flat T waves, and (with concurrent hypoK) U waves. A normal ECG does not exclude risk.If symptomatic / cardiac
24-h urine Mg or spot FEMgThe key branch point when the cause isn't obvious: in the face of hypomagnesemia, > 10–30 mg/day in urine (or FEMg > 2%) = renal wasting; < 2% = the kidney is conserving, so the loss is GI / redistribution / intake.To localize
Consider Gitelman workupYoung adult with hypomagnesemia + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis + low urine calcium and normal BP → suspect Gitelman syndrome (thiazide-like tubulopathy); refer nephrology / genetics.If tubulopathy
Medication + diet reviewPPIs, loop/thiazide diuretics, alcohol, cisplatin, cetuximab, aminoglycosides, amphotericin, calcineurin inhibitors, foscarnet — the history often is the diagnosis.Every visit
How the number can lieFalsely reassuring: a normal serum Mg can hide a large deficit because < 1% of body Mg is extracellular — the "normal" is the doorknob, not the house. Falsely low / spurious: hemolysis, EDTA/citrate tube contamination, and hemodilution can distort the value; a chronically ill or malnourished patient with a "normal" Mg but refractory hypokalemia is depleted until proven otherwise (some use a magnesium retention/loading test to prove it). Transiently low: acute redistribution (refeeding, insulin, catecholamines, post-parathyroidectomy hungry bone) drops the number without net loss.

Calculator · Fractional excretion of magnesium (FEMg) — renal vs extrarenal

On a spot urine + paired serum, FEMg = (UMg × SCr) / (0.7 × SMg × UCr) × 100. The 0.7 corrects for the ~30% of serum Mg that is protein-bound and not filtered. In a hypomagnesemic patient, FEMg > 2% means the kidney is inappropriately wasting Mg (renal cause); < 2% means it is appropriately conserving (GI / intake / shift). Enter UMg and SMg in the same unit and UCr and SCr in the same unit.

FEMg

These are decision aids, not a substitute for judgment or your institution's protocol. No validated numeric severity score exists for hypomagnesemia. For related, verifiable tools link out to MDCalc (e.g., a QTc / Bazett calculator to quantify the torsades risk that low Mg creates).

Treat

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

The governing principle: match the fix to the cause, and choose the salt for tolerability. Oral magnesium repletion is slow (bone equilibrates over days–weeks) and its main limit is diarrhea — which itself wastes magnesium — so the art is picking a well-absorbed, non-cathartic salt and dividing the dose. For ongoing renal wasting you can't out-supplement (Gitelman, cisplatin, calcineurin inhibitors), add a potassium-sparing diuretic (amiloride) to plug the leak. And whatever the cause, deprescribe the offender where you can — the single most effective outpatient intervention is often stopping an unnecessary PPI.
1
Diet, deprescribe the offender, and oral magnesium salts
First move for mild–moderate asymptomatic outpatient hypomagnesemia.
▾
Oral Mg refills the deficit; dietary magnesium sustains it; stopping the PPI/diuretic removes the drain. A sustained-release or well-chelated salt (glycinate, chloride, lactate) is absorbed better and causes less diarrhea than magnesium oxide.
  • Dietary magnesium — nuts and seeds (pumpkin, almonds), legumes, whole grains, leafy greens, dark chocolate. Good for prevention and mild cases, but diet alone rarely corrects an established deficit with ongoing losses.
  • Deprescribe / substitute the cause — stop an unnecessary PPI (or switch to an H2-blocker), lower or potassium-spare the diuretic, treat the diarrhea.
  • Oral magnesium salt — see the dose table; divide the total daily dose (2–4×) to improve absorption and limit diarrhea.
Seeds, nuts, legumes, whole grains, and leafy greens are the richest dietary magnesium — the backbone of prevention and mild repletion (a deficit with ongoing loss still needs a supplement).
Mk2010, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — File:Pumpkin Seeds.jpg
Oral magnesium salts differ enormously in elemental Mg content and GI tolerability. Well-chelated/sustained-release forms (glycinate, chloride, lactate) beat magnesium oxide, which is poorly absorbed and the most cathartic.
Kulmalukko, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — File:Magnesium tablets.jpg

If the prior dose/formulation is unknown, start a well-tolerated sustained-release salt at a modest divided dose (e.g., magnesium chloride ~128 mg elemental BID), recheck Mg (and K⁺/Ca²⁺, creatinine) in ~1–2 weeks, and titrate. Do not resume a large empiric dose, especially if renal function has changed — over-repletion causes hypermagnesemia (worse in CKD).
2
Add a potassium-sparing diuretic for ongoing renal wasting
When the kidney keeps leaking Mg despite oral repletion.
▾
Amiloride (and, less commonly, triamterene or spironolactone) blocks the ENaC sodium channel in the collecting duct. That reduces the lumen-negative electrical gradient that drives distal magnesium (and potassium) secretion — so the kidney retains more of what you supplement. It is the mechanistic tool for renal wasters you can't out-dose.
DrugStartTitration → target / maxWhy it works / when to pickCaution / alternative
Amiloride (ENaC blocker) — default5 mg PO dailyTitrate to 10 mg (max ~20 mg) daily to Mg/K⁺ responseReduces distal Mg and K⁺ wasting — the agent of choice for Gitelman, cisplatin/calcineurin-inhibitor wasting, and diuretic-induced lossHyperkalemia risk (monitor, esp. CKD/RAASi); avoid stacking K-sparers
Spironolactone / eplerenone (MRA)Spironolactone 12.5–25 mg dailyTitrate to effect (25–50 mg)Alternative K/Mg-sparer, especially with secondary hyperaldosteronism or when an MRA is otherwise indicatedGynecomastia (spironolactone) → eplerenone; monitor K⁺
3
Cause-directed & specialist therapy
Treat the driver; refer when the mechanism needs it.
▾
  • PPI-associated: discontinue or step down to the lowest effective dose / switch to an H2-blocker; magnesium often normalizes within weeks (FDA 2011 safety communication). If the PPI is truly required, co-supplement and add amiloride.
  • Gitelman / Bartter: high-dose oral Mg (divided to limit diarrhea) + oral K⁺, an ENaC blocker or MRA, and cause-specific care — nephrology/genetics co-management.
  • Chemotherapy (cisplatin, cetuximab/EGFR inhibitors): anticipate and monitor; aggressive oral ± IV repletion during cycles; amiloride reduces cisplatin-induced renal wasting. Coordinate with oncology.
  • Alcohol use disorder: multifactorial (poor intake, GI loss, renal wasting, refeeding) — replete Mg, treat the disorder, and anticipate a further drop during refeeding.
  • Malabsorption / short gut / chronic diarrhea: treat the GI disease; higher divided oral doses, IV if oral can't keep up.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to watch

🔗

How comorbidities change the course and the management

ComorbidityEffect on hypomagnesemiaHow it changes management
Refractory hypokalemiaLow Mg disinhibits ROMK → renal K⁺ wasting that will not correct with KCl aloneReplace Mg first/with K⁺. Any potassium that "won't hold" = check and correct magnesium
Refractory hypocalcemiaSevere Mg depletion impairs PTH secretion + causes PTH resistance → hypocalcemia resistant to Ca/vitamin DGive Mg — calcium normalizes as PTH function returns; don't chase it with calcium alone
Heart failure / on diureticsLoop/thiazides waste Mg and K⁺; low Mg is arrhythmogenic and worsens digoxin toxicityMonitor Mg with K⁺; keep Mg > 2.0 in arrhythmia/HF; consider a K/Mg-sparing agent rather than escalating supplements
Digoxin therapyHypomagnesemia (like hypokalemia) potentiates digoxin binding to Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → toxicity even at "therapeutic" levelsKeep Mg (and K⁺) replete; give empiric Mg for digoxin-associated arrhythmia
Type 2 diabetesOsmotic diuresis + tubular dysfunction cause renal Mg wasting; low Mg worsens insulin resistance (a two-way street)Screen and replete; watch for further loss with SGLT2/loop use and during DKA treatment
Alcohol use disorderThe classic multifactorial cause (intake, diarrhea, renal wasting) — and refeeding drops it furtherReplete Mg early (it also eases withdrawal/arrhythmia risk); anticipate the refeeding dip
CKDThe opposite risk — impaired excretion means over-repletion causes hypermagnesemiaReplete cautiously: reduce dose ~50% when eGFR/CrCl < 30, smaller boluses, recheck sooner
Drugs that cause or worsen hypomagnesemia (review & deprescribe where possible): proton-pump inhibitors (long-term — FDA 2011 warning) · loop & thiazide diuretics · aminoglycosides · amphotericin B · cisplatin/carboplatin · cetuximab & other EGFR inhibitors · calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) · foscarnet · pentamidine · high-dose β2-agonists (shift) · and alcohol. Use with caution in a magnesium-depleted patient: QT-prolonging drugs (many antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, ondansetron) and digoxin — low Mg (often with low K⁺) multiplies their torsades and toxicity risk, so correct Mg and K⁺ before/with them.
Monitor

Titration & follow-up

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • After starting/changing oral repletion: recheck Mg (with K⁺, Ca²⁺, creatinine) in ~1–2 weeks — remember the serum lags total-body stores, so keep supplementing a while after the number normalizes.
  • Starting or continuing a PPI/diuretic/nephrotoxin: periodic Mg (and K⁺); the FDA advises checking Mg before starting and during long-term PPI therapy in at-risk patients.
  • Starting amiloride / an MRA: check K⁺ and creatinine at ~1 and 4 weeks — now watch for hyperkalemia, especially with CKD or RAASi.
  • Recurrent/refractory hypomagnesemia: re-verify adherence and formulation (switch off oxide), quantify the renal loss (FEMg), and reconsider Gitelman or an ongoing drug cause before simply increasing the dose.
  • The bedside monitor of overshoot is the deep tendon reflexes — diminished reflexes are the earliest sign of hypermagnesemia.
Prevent

Prevention & screening context

🛡️

What the evidence does — and does not — recommend

On USPSTFThere is no USPSTF Grade A or B recommendation specific to hypomagnesemia — it is a laboratory consequence of other conditions and drugs, not a screening target. The most relevant Grade A/B items are indirect: screening & brief counseling for unhealthy alcohol use (Grade B), a leading cause of magnesium depletion; and screening for hypertension (Grade A) and using diuretics rationally. The FDA's 2011 PPI-magnesium safety communication is the closest thing to a formal prevention directive.
GradeRecommendationRelevance to hypomagnesemia
BScreen & brief behavioral counseling for unhealthy alcohol use in adultsAlcohol use disorder → poor intake, GI loss, and renal Mg wasting → recurrent hypomagnesemia
AScreen for hypertension in adults ≥ 18Rational diuretic use (and detecting Gitelman-like presentations) reduces iatrogenic Mg/K⁺ wasting
BScreen for type 2 diabetes / prediabetes (35–70, overweight)Diabetes causes renal Mg wasting; low Mg worsens insulin resistance — a modifiable loop

Prevention essentials (highest yield first)

  • Deprescribe unnecessary PPIs and use the lowest effective dose/duration; check Mg in long-term users.
  • Anticipate drug-induced loss — pair a chronic loop/thiazide with monitoring; check Mg during cisplatin/cetuximab/aminoglycoside/amphotericin courses.
  • Replace Mg alongside K⁺ in anyone with recurrent hypokalemia — the two deficits travel together.
  • Dietary counseling (nuts, seeds, legumes, greens, whole grains) for at-risk and recurrent patients.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED / admit for any of: Mg < 1.0–1.2 mg/dL; tetany, seizures, or carpopedal spasm; any arrhythmia, prolonged QT, or torsades; hypomagnesemia in a patient on digoxin or with significant heart disease; severe refractory hypokalemia or hypocalcemia; an ongoing rapid loss (severe diarrhea, high-output stoma, chemo course) or an inability to take/absorb oral magnesium; or a level that cannot be safely rechecked as an outpatient.
A patient with carpopedal spasm and a long QT does not get an oral prescription and a follow-up — that is monitored IV magnesium in the ED, because the next event can be torsades.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient repletion
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Hypomagnesemia is frequently an inpatient finding (prevalence ~10–12% of hospitalized patients). Admit — usually to a monitored bed / telemetry — for any of:

  • Mg < 1.0–1.2 mg/dL, or any level with symptoms.
  • Tetany, seizures, or overt neuromuscular irritability.
  • ECG changes (prolonged QT, widened QRS) or any arrhythmia — especially torsades.
  • Refractory hypokalemia or hypocalcemia that won't correct without magnesium.
  • Hypomagnesemia on digoxin or with significant structural heart disease.
  • An ongoing large loss (severe diarrhea, high-output stoma/NG, chemo) or inability to take/absorb oral magnesium.
Frame the case by level × symptoms × ECG × companions × cause. A stable 1.4 mg/dL in a well patient on a PPI is oral repletion and deprescribing; a 0.9 with a long QT, or a magnesium that is the reason a potassium won't rise, is a monitored bed with IV magnesium.

Treat

Acute management — repletion done right

💊

Replete → slow the infusion to keep the dose → fix the companions (exact doses)

If there is torsades, seizure, or tetany: give IV magnesium sulfate 1–2 g over 1–2 minutes (torsades) or over 10–15 minutes (seizure/tetany), then an infusion — this is a monitored, IV emergency. Replete K⁺ and Ca²⁺ concurrently and get continuous ECG. (See the ICU panel for the full arrhythmia algorithm.)
1
① IV magnesium sulfate — moderate–severe or symptomatic
The inpatient workhorse; the trick is the infusion rate.
▾
IV magnesium refills the deficit directly. The counter-intuitive rule: infuse slowly. A rapid rise in serum Mg blows past the renal reabsorptive threshold and up to ~50% of a fast bolus is excreted in the urine — so for repletion you give it over hours (usual rate ~1–2 g/hr, and slower still favors retention; do not exceed ~9 g/hr) to actually retain the magnesium. Fast pushes are reserved for torsades/seizure.
IV magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄). 1 g MgSO₄ ≈ 98 mg (4 mmol, 8 mEq) elemental Mg — so a "2 g" dose delivers ~8 mmol. Diluted in saline/D5W and infused by pump.
U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain — 50% Magnesium Sulfate Injection, USP
Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate (Epsom salt) — the same molecule given IV in the hospital and taken orally (a cathartic) at home. Its low elemental fraction (~10%) is why oral MgSO₄ is a laxative more than a repletion salt.
Wikimedia Commons, Public domain — File:Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate.jpg
SeverityDose (MgSO₄)Rate / howWhy / targetCaution
Severe / symptomatic (< 1.0 mg/dL, tetany, arrhythmia)4–8 g total over 12–24 h (e.g., 2 g doses)~1–2 g/hr (slower favors retention; faster only for torsades/seizure); dilute (e.g., 1 g/100 mL)Refills a large deficit while staying under the renal spill threshold; target Mg > 1.5–2.0Reduce ~50% and slow further if CrCl < 30; watch reflexes/BP
Moderate (1.0–1.5 mg/dL)2–4 g IVOver 4–12 h (~1–2 g/hr)Steady repletion; oral once tolerating and level stabilizingPhlebitis if concentrated peripherally — dilute
Torsades / seizure / eclampsia1–2 g IV (eclampsia: 4–6 g load)Over 1–2 min (torsades) or 10–20 min; then infusion 0.5–1 g/hr (eclampsia 1–2 g/hr)Membrane stabilization terminates torsades even when serum Mg is "normal"Continuous ECG; monitor for hypermagnesemia (areflexia, resp depression) — esp. renal impairment

Dose ranges reflect standard hospital references (StatPearls; AAFP magnesium reviews; EMCrit/IBCC; product labeling). Serum Mg lags — recheck ~6–12 h after IV and daily, and keep replacing after it normalizes because the intracellular/bone deficit persists. Confirm against your institution's protocol.

2
② Oral magnesium — mild, and to sustain after IV
Because IV boluses partly wash out, oral is the retention strategy.
▾
Once the patient tolerates PO and isn't peri-arrhythmic, oral magnesium (sustained-release chloride/lactate, or glycinate for tolerability) sustains repletion better than repeated washed-out IV boluses. Divide the dose to limit diarrhea.
  • Sustained-release magnesium chloride/lactate ~ 64–128 mg elemental BID, or magnesium glycinate ~120–240 mg elemental/day divided; titrate to Mg > 2.0.
  • Avoid magnesium oxide for repletion if diarrhea is limiting — it is poorly absorbed and the most cathartic.
  • Continue oral repletion several days beyond a normal serum level to refill intracellular/bone stores.
3
③ Fix the companions & stop the loss
The reasons the numbers won't budge.
▾
If the K⁺ or Ca²⁺ won't correct, the cause is almost always unreplaced magnesium. If the Mg itself won't hold, there is an ongoing loss (continuing diuresis/diarrhea, chemo, unremoved PPI) or renal wasting that needs amiloride.
  • Potassium & calcium: replete concurrently, but understand they follow the magnesium — don't over-chase them in isolation.
  • Stop the drain: hold/adjust the diuretic, deprescribe the PPI, treat the diarrhea, coordinate chemo dosing.
  • Renal wasting that persists: add amiloride 5–10 mg/day to reduce distal Mg (and K⁺) loss.
Calculator · Hypomagnesemia severity & action

Combines the level, symptoms, ECG, and renal function into a band and the immediate action. Any tetany, seizure, or arrhythmia raises the urgency regardless of the number; reduced renal function caps the dose.

Assessment
—
Monitor

What to trend

📈

Recheck, and watch for overshoot

  • Recheck Mg ~6–12 h after IV and at least daily during active repletion — the serum lags and boluses partly wash out, so trend it rather than trusting a single value.
  • Trend K⁺ and Ca²⁺ — they should start correcting once Mg is replaced; if they don't, the Mg isn't yet adequate.
  • Telemetry until Mg > 1.5 and stable and the QT/ECG has normalized.
  • Watch for hypermagnesemia, especially in renal impairment: the earliest sign is loss of deep tendon reflexes (~8–12 mg/dL / 4–5 mmol/L), then hypotension and flushing, then respiratory depression (~12–18 mg/dL) and heart block/cardiac arrest at higher levels — check reflexes each shift during aggressive IV repletion.
  • Reassess the ongoing loss (diuresis, diarrhea, chemo) and whether the offending drug can be stopped.
Write a clear "next Mg due at [time]" order and check the reflexes. The two classic errors are declaring victory on the first normal serum level (the stores are still empty) and pushing IV Mg too fast (you excrete most of it, and in CKD you cause hypermagnesemia).
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers

Escalate to ICU when: torsades de pointes or any sustained ventricular arrhythmia; status epilepticus / recurrent seizures from hypomagnesemia; respiratory compromise from tetany/laryngospasm; hemodynamic instability; eclampsia requiring high-dose magnesium infusion with monitoring; or digoxin toxicity with arrhythmia. Also escalate if repletion needs continuous ECG and titration beyond floor capability.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: Mg > 1.5 mg/dL and stable on oral repletion (no ongoing IV need), K⁺ and Ca²⁺ corrected, ECG/QT normalized, symptoms resolved, the cause identified and addressed (PPI deprescribed, diuretic adjusted, chemo plan coordinated, amiloride started for renal wasting), a clear oral supplement + monitoring plan, and a follow-up Mg within ~1–2 weeks (with K⁺/Ca²⁺/creatinine).

Home

Stable Mg, reversible cause fixed, reliable follow-up labs arranged.

Home health

Needs in-home lab draws / medication management (frail, complex regimen, new amiloride).

SNF

Medically stable but needs skilled nursing / monitored medication administration.

IRF / acute rehab

Deconditioning or resolving neuromuscular sequelae needing ≥ 3h therapy/day.

Behavioral health / addiction

Alcohol use disorder driving recurrence — arrange treatment and nutrition support.

Nephrology / oncology clinic

Gitelman, cisplatin/cetuximab or calcineurin-inhibitor wasting needing specialist follow-up.
🫀 ICU — arrhythmia, eclampsia & critical repletion
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Hypomagnesemia is the most common electrolyte abnormality in the ICU (~50–65%) and an independent marker of higher mortality — but the reasons to be in the unit are its lethal complications:

  • Torsades de pointes or any sustained ventricular arrhythmia (the signature emergency).
  • Status epilepticus / recurrent seizures attributable to hypomagnesemia.
  • Eclampsia (or severe pre-eclampsia) requiring magnesium loading + infusion with monitoring.
  • Tetany with laryngospasm or respiratory compromise.
  • Digoxin toxicity with arrhythmia; severe refractory hypokalemia/hypocalcemia with instability.
Torsades de pointes is a peri-arrest rhythm: give IV magnesium sulfate 1–2 g over 1–2 min (repeat once if needed) — it terminates torsades even when serum Mg is normal — replete K⁺ to ≥ 4.0–4.5, stop any QT-prolonging drug, and prepare for defibrillation/overdrive pacing.
Torsades de pointes — polymorphic VT with the QRS axis "twisting" around the baseline, arising from a prolonged QT. IV magnesium is first-line and works regardless of the serum Mg level. Low Mg (usually with low K⁺) is a classic, correctable substrate.
Jer5150, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — File:Torsades de Pointes TdP.png
A normal 12-lead for comparison — quantify the substrate with the corrected QT (Bazett). Low Mg prolongs the QT (compounded by the hypokalemia/hypocalcemia it causes), and a long QT is the runway for torsades.
邱鈺鋒, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — File:10sec-ekg-12-lead.jpg
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous cardiac monitoring; defibrillator/pacing pads on the patient for torsades/arrhythmia.
  • Reliable IV access for magnesium infusions; central access if concentrated/rapid or with vasoactive needs; arterial line if unstable.
  • Serial Mg (± ionized Mg where available) plus K⁺, ionized Ca²⁺, phosphate, and glucose; correcting Mg is part of fixing all of them.
  • Target Mg > 2.0 mg/dL in active arrhythmia, digoxin toxicity, or eclampsia; keep K⁺ ≥ 4.0–4.5.
  • Bedside toxicity check: deep tendon reflexes each assessment — areflexia is the sentinel of hypermagnesemia. In eclampsia, follow reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output; keep the therapeutic magnesium window (~4.8–8.4 mg/dL) and have calcium gluconate ready as the antidote.
Replete

Therapeutic magnesium — the ICU regimens

💉

Magnesium as a drug: arrhythmia, eclampsia, bronchospasm

In the unit, magnesium is not just a level to fix — it is a therapeutic agent given for its membrane-stabilizing effect, sometimes regardless of the serum value. The regimens below are the high-yield ICU uses. Rates and totals must be tempered by renal function.

IndicationMechanism / roleDose & routeEffect / targetCautions
Torsades de pointesSuppresses early afterdepolarizations; stabilizes myocardial membrane1–2 g IV over 1–2 min, repeat once PRN; then 0.5–1 g/hr infusionTerminates torsades even if serum Mg normal; also correct K⁺ ≥ 4.0–4.5Continuous ECG; watch for hypermagnesemia if repeated / renal impairment
Severe/symptomatic depletionRefills the cofactor; enables K⁺/Ca²⁺ correction4–8 g over 12–24 h (~1–2 g/hr; slower favors retention)Mg > 1.5–2.0; K⁺/Ca²⁺ followSlow infusion to avoid renal washout; halve dose if CrCl < 30
Eclampsia / severe pre-eclampsiaCerebral vasospasm relief + seizure threshold (NMDA modulation)Load 4–6 g IV over 15–20 min, then 1–2 g/hr infusion (per MAGPIE / obstetric protocols); recurrent seizure: 2–4 gHalves eclampsia risk (MAGPIE); target seizure controlReflexes/RR/urine output; calcium gluconate antidote; reduce with renal impairment
Severe asthma / bronchospasmSmooth-muscle relaxation (Ca²⁺ antagonism) — adjunct2 g IV over 20 min (single dose) in severe exacerbations not responding to standard therapyModest ↑ in lung function / ↓ admissions in the sickestAdjunct only; not a substitute for bronchodilators/steroids
Digoxin-associated arrhythmiaCounters the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase impairment that low Mg/K⁺ worsen1–2 g IV; correct K⁺; digoxin-specific antibody for life-threatening toxicityRhythm stabilizationCaution in AV block/bradycardia; renal dosing
Everything here maps to the mechanism: magnesium stabilizes the membrane (torsades, seizures, bronchospasm) and restores the cofactor (letting K⁺ and Ca²⁺ correct). The recurring caveat is renal: because the kidney is the only fast exit for magnesium, impaired excretion turns a therapeutic dose into hypermagnesemia — so titrate to reflexes and the level, and keep calcium gluconate at hand.

Eclampsia dosing per the MAGPIE trial (Lancet 2002) and obstetric guidelines; asthma per severe-exacerbation evidence; torsades/repletion per ACLS, EMCrit/IBCC, and StatPearls. Verify against local protocol — magnesium infusions are high-alert in renal impairment.

Source

Special causes & source control

🎯

When the cause changes the plan

CauseSpecific therapyKey point
Refeeding syndromeReplace Mg, phosphate, and K⁺; reintroduce calories slowly; thiamine firstThe insulin surge pulls Mg/PO₄/K⁺ into cells at once — a low Mg here compounds lethal hypophosphatemia and arrhythmia.
Alcohol withdrawal / DTsAggressive Mg repletion (also eases irritability/arrhythmia); treat withdrawal; anticipate refeedingMultifactorial depletion is near-universal; check and replace early even with a "borderline" level.
DKA / HHS treatmentReplace Mg alongside K⁺ and phosphate as insulin drives them intracellularlyOsmotic diuresis depletes Mg; insulin unmasks it — trend the whole electrolyte family.
Post-cardiac-surgeryProphylactic/therapeutic IV Mg to reduce post-op atrial fibrillation and ventricular ectopyMeta-analyses support magnesium for post-op AF prophylaxis; keep Mg replete perioperatively.
Cisplatin / cetuximab / calcineurin inhibitorsAnticipate renal wasting; aggressive repletion; add amiloride to cut the lossThe wasting persists for weeks–months after the drug; may need sustained oral Mg + amiloride.
Hungry bone syndrome (post-parathyroidectomy)Replace Mg with Ca²⁺ and phosphate as bone avidly re-mineralizesA redistribution cause — the deficit can be large and abrupt; monitor closely.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when Mg is rising steadily toward > 1.5 mg/dL on non-emergent repletion, no arrhythmia off continuous monitoring, the QT has normalized, seizures/tetany have resolved, K⁺ and Ca²⁺ are correcting, and (for eclampsia) the obstetric course allows. Transition IV → oral once tolerating.
Not yet if…there is ongoing torsades risk (still-prolonged QT, unremoved QT-prolonging drug, persistent hypokalemia), an ongoing large loss (active chemo, high-output GI), the magnesium is only transiently up during an active infusion, or the patient remains on digoxin with an unstable rhythm. Keep on telemetry until the trend is convincingly stable at target without emergent infusion.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The things that change what you do

  1. Refractory hypokalemia is hypomagnesemia until proven otherwise. Low intracellular Mg disinhibits ROMK, so the kidney wastes potassium no matter how much KCl you give — check and replace Mg, and the K⁺ finally holds.
  2. Refractory hypocalcemia, too. Severe hypomagnesemia shuts down PTH secretion and creates PTH resistance; the calcium won't correct with calcium or vitamin D until magnesium is repleted.
  3. Give empiric magnesium in torsades — 1–2 g IV — regardless of the serum level. It terminates torsades by suppressing early afterdepolarizations, not by "correcting a number."
  4. A normal serum Mg does not exclude depletion. Less than 1% of body magnesium is extracellular; a malnourished or chronically ill patient with a "normal" Mg and refractory hypokalemia is depleted (consider a retention test).
  5. Slow the infusion to keep the dose. A rapid IV bolus overshoots the renal reabsorptive threshold and up to ~50% is excreted in the urine — for repletion, give over hours (≤ 1 g/hr) so the magnesium is actually retained.
  6. Check a magnesium in every chronic PPI patient with cramps, palpitations, or an unexplained low K⁺/Ca²⁺ — PPIs down-regulate intestinal TRPM6/7 (FDA 2011 warning), and deprescribing is curative.
  7. Magnesium is not on the BMP. The most common reason it's missed is simply that nobody ordered it — send it deliberately in the at-risk.
  8. Watch the reflexes. The earliest bedside sign of iatrogenic hypermagnesemia is loss of deep tendon reflexes — especially in CKD, where the dose ceiling is much lower (halve it below CrCl 30).
  9. Digoxin + low Mg = danger. Hypomagnesemia (usually with hypokalemia) potentiates digoxin toxicity; keep both replete and give Mg for dig-associated arrhythmia.
  10. Use FEMg to localize: in a hypomagnesemic patient, FEMg > 2% = renal wasting; < 2% = GI/intake/shift (the kidney is appropriately conserving).
  11. Pick the salt for the gut. Magnesium oxide is cheap but poorly absorbed and the most cathartic; sustained-release chloride/lactate and glycinate are better tolerated and better retained — and diarrhea itself wastes magnesium.
  12. Amiloride plugs a renal leak you can't out-supplement (Gitelman, cisplatin, calcineurin inhibitors) by lowering the distal voltage that drives Mg/K⁺ secretion.
  13. Anticipate the drop. Refeeding, insulin for DKA, hungry-bone after parathyroidectomy, and catecholamine surges all shift magnesium into cells — replete proactively in these settings.
  14. Magnesium is a drug, not just a level. It's first-line for torsades, standard for eclampsia (MAGPIE: loading 4–6 g then 1–2 g/hr), and an adjunct in severe asthma (2 g IV) and post-op AF prophylaxis.
  15. Keep repleting after the number normalizes. The serum corrects before the intracellular/bone stores do — stop too early and it relapses.

Refs

Sources & guidelines

Guidelines & key reviews

There is no single dedicated major-society guideline for hypomagnesemia; the authoritative current sources are the reviews and references below (AJKD Core Curriculum 2024, StatPearls, Merck, IBCC/EMCrit, NHS SPS, NIH ODS, FDA, and AHA/ACLS for arrhythmia).

  • Van Laecke S, et al. Magnesium Disorders: Core Curriculum 2024. Am J Kidney Dis 2024;83(6):803–15 — the single best dedicated review (physiology, causes, FEMg, repletion). AJKD 2024
  • Ayuk J, Gittoes NJL. Treatment of hypomagnesaemia. Am J Kidney Dis 2014;63(4):691–5 — practical repletion (IV vs oral, salt selection, renal caution). PubMed 24485147
  • Agus ZS. Hypomagnesemia. J Am Soc Nephrol 1999;10(7):1616–22 — classic mechanistic review (renal handling, K⁺/Ca²⁺ interdependence). JASN 1999
  • Gragossian A, Bashir K, Bhutta BS, Friede R. Hypomagnesemia. StatPearls (2023) — definitions, causes, dosing, FEMg. NCBI Bookshelf
  • Ahmed F, Mohammed A. Magnesium: The Forgotten Electrolyte — A Review on Hypomagnesemia. Med Sci (Basel) 2019;7(4):56 — etiologies, presentation, management. PMC6524065
  • Internet Book of Critical Care (IBCC/EMCrit) — Hypomagnesemia — ICU repletion, torsades, infusion-rate physiology. emcrit.org/ibcc/hypomagnesemia
  • Huang C-L, Kuo E. Mechanism of Hypokalemia in Magnesium Deficiency. J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18(10):2649–52 — Mg block of ROMK (why hypokalemia is refractory). JASN 2007
  • FDA Drug Safety Communication (2011): Low magnesium levels can be associated with long-term use of proton pump inhibitors. fda.gov
  • Whang R, Ryder KW. Frequency of hypomagnesemia and hypermagnesemia. JAMA 1990;263(22):3063–4 — prevalence and the case for routine testing. PubMed 2342219
  • LITFL ECG Library — Hypomagnesaemia / Torsades de Pointes — ECG features and the magnesium response. litfl.com/magnesium

Landmark trials & evidence

Trial / studyYearResultWhy it matters
MAGPIE (Magpie Trial Collaborative Group, Lancet)2002IV magnesium sulfate halved the risk of eclampsia (RR ~0.42) vs placebo in women with pre-eclampsia, with no substantive harmEstablished magnesium as the standard for eclampsia prevention/treatment — the load-then-infuse regimen used in the ICU
Eclampsia Trial Collaborative Group1995Magnesium sulfate was superior to diazepam and to phenytoin for preventing recurrent eclamptic seizuresCemented magnesium (not conventional anticonvulsants) as the anti-eclampsia agent
ISIS-4 (Fourth International Study of Infarct Survival, Lancet)1995No mortality benefit from routine IV magnesium in ~58,000 acute MI patientsEnded routine magnesium in MI — magnesium is for the deficient and for specific arrhythmias, not empirically for everyone
Huang & Kuo (Mg deficiency & ROMK, JASN)2007Mg depletion releases the intracellular block of ROMK → renal K⁺ wasting refractory to K⁺ aloneThe physiologic basis for "always replace magnesium" in refractory hypokalemia
3Mg trial (Goodacre et al., severe acute asthma)2013IV/nebulized magnesium gave at most a modest benefit in severe asthma; not clearly superior overallFrames IV magnesium (2 g) as an adjunct in the sickest asthmatics, not a routine therapy
PPI–hypomagnesemia (FDA safety review; observational cohorts)2011+Long-term PPI use associated with clinically significant hypomagnesemia, often with hypokalemia/hypocalcemiaMade medication review (deprescribing PPIs) a first-line, curative intervention
Post-op AF meta-analyses (magnesium prophylaxis)variousPeri-operative IV magnesium reduces post-cardiac-surgery atrial fibrillationSupports keeping magnesium replete and prophylactic dosing around cardiac surgery

Note: much of hypomagnesemia repletion rests on physiology and consensus rather than large RCTs of repletion strategy; the trials above define the therapeutic uses of magnesium (eclampsia, asthma, arrhythmia) and the mechanistic basis for treating the deficiency.
